issues.title: THE BEAUTY OF AUTUMN
issues.subtitle: Berry lips, brown eyeliner, the return of red lipstick and the little rituals that make getting ready half the fun.

articles.title: The Autumn Beauty Edit
articles.excerpt: A darker lip, a little brown eyeliner and makeup that doesn’t need to look perfect.
articles.body:
The Autumn Beauty Edit

Autumn makeup is always a little more fun. After months of sunscreen, tinted moisturiser and whatever lip product was at the bottom of a beach bag, a darker lipstick suddenly feels right again.

This season, the shades to watch are cherry, wine and soft brown. Not necessarily worn all at once, and definitely not with the idea that everyone needs to buy an entirely new makeup bag. A berry stain tapped onto the lips can do more for an outfit than a complicated routine.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/0w4WM6_8tz_JVU4akXkE27QVV6boD34Lfciy7RYUKCqmj9eXWTF2R0_UZrVp-cgG0aJz13m3UZ_qGj3Rmvp88lWC_1A4KXIRReEBz0YzYn6JTj_IfLmSquOnE9TLAG5BKEqci83GKCI1zHFxOid3b_vbXlnuk_rLG4rRGgRs_WsoUBpCT21qLbJP13pt5S2T.jpeg]]

The 1990s references are still there, especially in the softly smudged brown eyeliner and neutral shadows. Think less perfect smoky eye, more makeup that looks even better a few hours after you put it on. A little colour close to the lash line, brushed-out brows and skin that still looks like skin are enough.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/bVWiDmM5TbC9qB_QiQjuyXktF2KOSR25R4VIRwmMi1dQkq9r1w3L2eSIVe_nZvEoP4rdt9XRDAoBFqG7ineyypJy2XciHd03LpmxtkWHKoreA5H-Nn3IbmG-kDAb8HCJDO2w0iNFZuDjr-Shu1NxTGjvfGSfu7w-Yf29WOyLZKq-DCWFULcP2EBpoFTpCJuE.jpeg]]

There's something refreshing about leaving texture alone, too. Freckles don't need covering, blush doesn't need to be perfectly placed, and a bit of shine isn't the end of the world. The best autumn looks have a slightly lived-in quality.

A deep red manicure or glossy, loosely styled hair fits the mood without demanding much effort. That's probably the nicest thing about the season's beauty direction: you can try a new shade, keep everything else familiar and still feel like you've changed things up.

articles.title: The Return of the Red Lip
articles.excerpt: From Old Hollywood to today’s blurred berry stains, there’s more than one way to wear red.
articles.body:
The Return of the Red Lip

A red lipstick has a way of making an ordinary outfit feel intentional. White shirt, jeans, hair pulled back, red lip. Suddenly it looks like you planned the whole thing.

The look has a long history, of course. Marilyn Monroe made bright red part of her Hollywood image, while the supermodels of the 1990s often went darker, pairing wine-toned lips with barely-there eyes or a smudged liner. Both versions still work, which says quite a lot about a colour that fashion keeps trying to reinvent.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/arlZpomvIhtXKT3Oi3Sokb5m1Z7M1OongB5RzfAxlI7YWiDVMv4I0kdhEpHr-xpRtpFHU6qxbmiVNTr06s5IuN5S-rzntuqMHe4UHYcfKumjtDxlefN2IKtQ2DRG5JW-VEHUUjgXFVeYIIFN36KmOBKBsEkZTOtspF--LhkAfXlg-fau6igVjO4fcwO5By6y.jpeg]]

Lately, I've been drawn to the softer interpretation: lipstick pressed on with a fingertip rather than applied in a perfect outline. Makeup artist Nina Park's blurred-lip technique has helped bring that look back into focus. It feels less formal, especially in berry and cranberry shades.

But there's room for the classic version too. A carefully lined crimson lip with clean skin and mascara has its own appeal. It's the kind of makeup that doesn't need much company.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/vRIaNPcpzUqQvia8zgE4NOunRngywv7jsKCDDjN7e971v5w5-7GTxQeT9DywYH2CfVKJT8GoJXxojXZn8Dvm_irHlSN5HdnD2PFVyYne2ByMp8seBRi7qsJ1Qr3Zj4ccZtcatcfph8mN411weTTLMaVTYEyMK2C0GUz70jQ2PYVhALHGHaKlkhT1G9933Bfw.jpeg]]

The trick is finding the red you actually want to wear. Some people love a bright, almost orange-red. Others prefer a deep cherry that could pass for their natural lip colour in dim light. There isn't a universally flattering answer, and that's what makes trying them on half the fun.

Red lipstick doesn't have to be saved for a special occasion. Sometimes the occasion is simply getting dressed.

articles.title: The Ritual of Getting Ready
articles.excerpt: The playlist, the perfume, the outfit changes. Sometimes the best part happens before you leave.
articles.body:
The Ritual of Getting Ready

Sometimes getting ready is better than the actual plan. There's music playing, three outfits on the bed, and someone texting to ask why you're still at home. Somehow, it's all part of the evening.

I love the small rituals: choosing a perfume, putting on jewellery, deciding whether the hair looks better up or down. None of it is particularly important on its own, but together it turns an ordinary Friday into something to look forward to.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/uYAMC0CZCDDDAJaIrg3EirmhthTTg0z-jINDTN_cupH6RwvE62S0zRiKeqKP8qiYftQAQOIizbXy01U1lXbYWIHyN8a_sBo7sAAkE9GujwLMN9An6CN7wFSn1r895z3AmyFhzfFkNzw2m_5kuf0FatEfkYyBP4_SNcsddRECWLnKEr87-yIPQT-ITtcv8KlO.jpeg]]

The dressing table has changed over the years. What once held powder compacts and silver brushes now shares space with phone chargers, lip liners and an open Pinterest board. The impulse is much the same, though. Getting ready gives us a little time to decide how we want to feel.

Fragrance is usually the final detail. Some perfumes belong to particular seasons, others to particular people. One spray can bring back a holiday, a dinner or a night you haven't thought about in ages.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/FDGH8hjmIR93O81QO5dTLTI7kcd41MkZkGfYwc1y9F0t9X1KbN95xWbtTQL8E-UlRH8-Zux6uL5Fk3OmmaZ8f5JCTPoZQsa7FiPoV1x4fxniAkPyf2WYqBV4Y22f8beEqR2rc2ItZoPUidMpX-JVDjZnoQoq7Q8jfpvmvz9fJAEwGckZTEBpN-IP5HZ16Q8U.jpeg]]

And getting ready with friends deserves its own category. Borrowed makeup, last-minute outfit swaps, someone insisting the first shoes were better. Those are often the moments that make it into the camera roll.

Not every day needs a full routine. But there's something nice about taking ten extra minutes for yourself, even when the only plan is dinner close to home.

issues.title: THE RIVIERA
issues.subtitle: A last look at the Riviera: Italian afternoons, Slim Aarons photographs and the summer clothes we keep coming back to.

articles.title: The Art of the Italian Summer
articles.excerpt: Long lunches, little harbours and the simple pleasures that make Italian summers hard to forget.
articles.body:
The Art of the Italian Summer

An Italian summer is made up of tiny details: the first coffee of the morning, towels hanging from balconies, boats nudging against the harbour and the question of where to have lunch taking up most of the afternoon.

Portofino looks almost unreal in photographs, with its pastel buildings crowded around the water. Capri has a different energy: busy little streets, dramatic cliffs, and sunglasses that somehow feel essential even in the shade. Both places have spent decades attracting people who want a particular version of summer.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/2mdB8CW00GSawB01KDRx74RFBfS65I9wVXEL6bhGrO1mHTl-EslRde6-MlJHCOwjrJ9yKUX6XNl-FI03JYc4ui_9gCE-pEa3Axh3cBrXM4MHsoXUpNwek1YNsRdG_w3yZh-JvaKPHybXfJKCgk9RtIVhpjNRCILdsb9XLw_Fwj5DCnSGnY944Pedm2VTtxnL.jpeg]]

The glamorous image has a history. During the middle of the twentieth century, Mediterranean resorts became gathering places for actors, artists and international travellers. Photographs of silk scarves, white trousers and long lunches helped build the fantasy we still associate with the Riviera.

But the best part of *la dolce vita* isn't really the glamour. It's the permission to enjoy an ordinary day. A late breakfast becomes a ritual. Lunch runs longer than expected. Nobody seems particularly concerned about checking the time.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/pfi3Vv4xFGvxmYJCRFPDYmTvfa1ViuABDjYb7b5yT4830qcS-ZzCgv4TlHCVVprhI_hj2a7K6nxvmWht65VF2GR5krrJZLA9HQpawJyMPlVoSqzEiafFkQy5P4mq5pX6KUwqFYY0PMS7aZvhP_9AY4oqswSaJvsljlA4rXywFu2YLXP9V5tzUGx2gdUDx4xm.jpeg]]

The clothes fit that rhythm: linen shirts, simple dresses, woven sandals and a scarf that works just as well in your hair as around your neck.

It's easy to romanticise the Italian summer, especially from somewhere else. Still, there's a good reason those images keep coming back. They remind us that a memorable day doesn't always need a complicated plan.

articles.title: Slim Aarons: Photographing the Beautiful Life
articles.excerpt: Pools, parasols and impossibly beautiful afternoons through the lens of Slim Aarons.
articles.body:
Slim Aarons: Photographing the Beautiful Life

If you've ever saved a photograph of a perfect poolside terrace, there's a good chance Slim Aarons had something to do with the way you imagine it.

His pictures are full of colour, sunlight and people who appear to have nowhere urgent to be. There are striped umbrellas, impossibly blue swimming pools, beautiful houses and guests dressed as though a photographer just happened to catch them looking their best.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/e482cd1Cj3Zit1ZVl0i30zSudIbniI2zxs4cUu70BWy1Btvs2JdH7nyOp0t2XxYr_7p98sltEx2IcmoFJm3Uqo5YVDxDcGCVKWU9j4CcoiAnlI0Njks9gmwZaGONrMzM4QJfUjj5cu61vFQUAXb803DoL56yRplIyQ9PqpmcWJU2uV_Fl8SyFBBxCKhfJ7qG.jpeg]]

Aarons began his career photographing war, before turning his camera towards the social world of the postwar decades. By the 1950s and 1960s, he was documenting holidays and private gatherings in places such as Capri, Palm Springs and the French Riviera.

His 1970 photograph *Poolside Gossip* is a good place to start. Taken at the Kaufmann Desert House, it shows an almost absurdly perfect meeting of architecture, fashion and afternoon light. Everything looks relaxed, even though the composition is carefully balanced.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/yARnB97cdEDSdh9GZFx56noOjIakGHnq1J-pyUzQjpTT0_uD_tvP5165kPIOgww7aQvdvlkIz2BXMvys49s5KdOLDJJr8A9tAl3xfpWHspQ-8-LV5bOQx0vwLVR5SdioJf2y7KeieCTGoJsj9WEXlSk8Ub9A8-qDrOkSJFgamSoc0Vdd8Z5-bN2TrZIiLRlW.jpeg]]

That's what makes his work interesting. The photographs feel spontaneous, but they're also incredibly precise. The architecture frames the people; the colours lead your eye; even the empty space matters.

Today, the influence is everywhere, from resort campaigns to hotel interiors and the vintage photographs pinned to summer moodboards. The lifestyle he captured was exclusive, not an everyday reality for most people. But the pictures still have a pull. They're less about a destination than the feeling of being somewhere you wish the afternoon would never end.

articles.title: The Riviera Wardrobe: An Enduring Elegance
articles.excerpt: Bardot, Jackie Kennedy and the summer pieces that never really leave our wardrobes.
articles.body:
The Riviera Wardrobe: An Enduring Elegance

The best summer outfits rarely involve very much. A white dress, flat sandals, a basket bag and good sunglasses can take you from breakfast to dinner without a second thought.

That easy approach to dressing is part of what made the French and Italian Rivieras so influential. In the 1950s and 1960s, women visiting Saint-Tropez and Capri began to look different from the way they dressed in the city. Clothes were lighter, silhouettes more relaxed and practicality suddenly looked chic.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/r9_JdLWUn6wBlyuxmrWy61FTFjppAlF1VCJW6gaXaztQCYIRPqN4Rwc_jsJN2P0LvFHVQumOA_c3sm8XxklzRVcfpJRurCC_PWzlJrsftU0-RygGuLSTWR7cyu2P1xjHOYG9ZhOoeIPARVMI7vw3bcg3RqTWn3ToOi6pUrTSXrXX1UwXlKf0C6jbtCwyaxM8.jpeg]]

Brigitte Bardot's gingham dresses and ballet flats became part of Saint-Tropez's visual identity. Jackie Kennedy offered another version in Capri: cropped trousers, silk scarves and oversized sunglasses. Their wardrobes weren't identical, but both showed how much personality can fit into simple pieces.

The fabrics matter. Cotton and linen feel right in the heat, and a silk scarf can make an outfit look finished without making it fussy. A little gold jewellery, a well-worn pair of sandals and a bag you don't mind carrying all day do the rest.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/ZnMAofYEYkobADOE-wHzXHTm-vWAW_4-AtDiKX_BO-L09P4wB6EUGqdGy-pqhSy5Ak-igSUlMcpp5fEtgA54W1c7TtORiBNZXw6hYqoPCiSrWAXXifE3hf0zZ1P3wHvonrpyP93Se0kTUizSzhM3oVmgsX9Vnxf4eDISKcx1tYjIGFhUavsf87yFag-tEpra.jpeg]]

What I like most about Riviera style is that it doesn't need to look new. A dress you've worn every summer, a vintage scarf or your favourite sunglasses often works better than an outfit bought for one photograph.

It's summer dressing at its easiest, which is probably why we keep returning to it.

issues.title: THE JEWELLERY
issues.subtitle: Cartier panthers, favourite heirlooms and the women who made some of history’s most memorable jewels their own.

articles.title: The Cartier Panthère: An Icon of Timeless Luxury
articles.excerpt: How Jeanne Toussaint turned a wild animal into Cartier’s most recognisable character.
articles.body:
The Cartier Panthère: An Icon of Timeless Luxury

A panther isn't the most obvious choice for a jewellery house. It's wild, a little intimidating and not particularly interested in looking delicate. Maybe that's why Cartier's version has lasted so long.

The motif appeared in Cartier's world in 1914, first through spotted patterns and illustrations. But it was Jeanne Toussaint, who became artistic director of the house's high jewellery department in 1933, who really gave the animal its personality.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/CN00034792.webp]]

Under her direction, panthers began to climb across brooches, curl around bracelets and perch on extraordinary gemstones. They looked alert and almost alive, rather than simply decorative.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/Cartier-Panther.jpg]]

One of the best-known examples was made for the Duchess of Windsor in 1949: a diamond-and-sapphire panther resting above a large sapphire. It's dramatic, certainly, but also surprisingly playful. The animal seems ready to move.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/wilT6DJwqholwMECUL-gjtsV9QuqFVDRygP_veJ_t47eifNLyxV7YL53_XDP0uLswpm-UBYqgLw-M37sGet5Bgo1WPRxSrH1lq3IGQJ2wDwsYf2Xe_iw7eftnLz_96M2djLbL2rVVQu17SuhA2e_shkB7OVSjGIgulu7QFXLy2y8aZA2c367SDh9MtrlYOI2.jpeg]]

Look closely at a Panthère piece and the workmanship becomes the story. Tiny stones create the spotted coat, a pair of coloured eyes changes the expression, and the angle of a paw can make a rigid piece of jewellery feel animated.

Cartier has returned to the panther again and again, from realistic sculptural designs to simpler outlines. The details change, but the attitude doesn't. It remains jewellery for someone who doesn't mind being noticed.

articles.title: The Art of the Heirloom
articles.excerpt: On lucky charms, Van Cleef & Arpels and the jewellery we hold on to for reasons beyond its value.
articles.body:
The Art of the Heirloom

My favourite thing about old jewellery is that it comes with a past. A ring might have been worn to a wedding, a necklace kept for special dinners, a bracelet put on every morning for years. Even when you don't know the full story, you can feel that it has one.

Van Cleef & Arpels understands the appeal of jewellery with meaning. Founded in Paris in 1906, the house has long drawn on flowers, butterflies, good-luck symbols and other small details from nature.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/francoisehardy-1-1024x802.jpg]]

The Alhambra collection, introduced in 1968, is perhaps its most familiar design. The original long necklace featured twenty clover-inspired motifs, framed with tiny golden beads. It was simple enough to wear every day, but distinctive enough to recognise instantly.

The clover wasn't chosen at random. Jacques Arpels was known for collecting four-leaf clovers and giving them to people as little wishes for good fortune. It's a lovely idea to carry into a piece of jewellery.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/0bc70269a0a43dcaed143b06d008a023.jpg]]

The design has since appeared in mother-of-pearl, onyx, malachite and other materials. Some versions are quiet; others are much more colourful. The shape stays familiar, even as the pieces take on different personalities.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/iMPupAVpTF83pe4kfN9Jhi-1920-80.jpg.webp]]

Of course, an heirloom doesn't need a famous name or an expensive stone. The most meaningful pieces are often the ones you associate with someone. A small pendant from a grandmother can matter far more than something valuable bought yesterday.

That's what makes jewellery different from so many other things we own. It can outlast a trend, travel between generations and still feel personal to the next person who wears it.

articles.title: Diamonds, Icons & the Women Who Wore Them
articles.excerpt: Elizabeth Taylor, Grace Kelly and Princess Diana each had their own way of wearing extraordinary jewels.
articles.body:
Diamonds, Icons & the Women Who Wore Them

Some jewellery is famous because of the stone. Other pieces are remembered because of the person wearing it. Elizabeth Taylor, Grace Kelly and Princess Diana understood that distinction better than most.

Taylor loved jewellery openly and enthusiastically. Her collection included the 33.19-carat Krupp Diamond, given to her by Richard Burton in 1968, and the historic La Peregrina pearl. She didn't treat these pieces like museum objects. She wore them, talked about them and clearly enjoyed them.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/elizabeth_taylore_wearing_bulgari_emerald_jewellery.jpg__1536x0_q75_crop-scale_subsampling-2_upscale-false.jpg]]

Grace Kelly's approach was quieter. Her Cartier engagement ring, with its approximately 10.47-carat emerald-cut diamond, was spectacular, but it suited her restrained style. Even with royal jewellery, she had a way of letting the clothes, the jewels and the person work together.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/DXzBdOpKk8gYgrD1VzAVwwRXCWCF35nKVAKvRr5iM35sPzAMRx8dAV11bwY3-UvA-quz0suvhPjSBK4HhGBH6xDdJLwyjdjypKIUV7Ry4BcESAviCtDDkJbGDcTBM3otB14vozBR3pv3niD-bzxf0vuXeAe3FYkCR5Cgrz8GKqveIEGnah5F4_QVyY6raxm6.jpeg]]

Diana brought something else: a willingness to experiment. Her sapphire engagement ring became one of the most recognisable pieces of royal jewellery, but I find her less conventional choices just as interesting. In 1985, she wore an emerald-and-diamond choker across her forehead during a visit to Australia. It was unexpected and completely memorable.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/ZHP-KVRPfWKc0xQ-6DCBRrs6yK7OyHR535DkUjUgQOM4UJqIDKPGtLCx4IcGsVhm1LaS8NKscJ1QP-jpaa1Zbj8I-SXPCt01gWvKrWlosndrvJxSUTYZnwWsWFR4k2RHLPW1pfblB6gMRvuFZQuaOzzE2sNaiDYyC82rA1aT26pi0izBTH35LaJfd6TZnNgX.jpeg]]

These women didn't have the same taste. Taylor loved theatrical glamour, Kelly favoured restraint and Diana often challenged the rules. That's precisely why their jewellery photographs remain so interesting.

The stones may be extraordinary, but it's the styling, the occasion and the person behind each piece that make the images worth revisiting.

issues.title: THE COUTURE
issues.subtitle: Inside the world of couture, from Chanel’s archive to the extraordinary work happening behind the runway.

articles.title: The Art of Couture
articles.excerpt: Beyond the runway: the hands, fittings and tiny details that bring couture to life.
articles.body:
The Art of Couture

It's easy to look at a couture show and focus on the finished dress. The dramatic entrance, the embroidery catching the light, the photographs that appear everywhere the next morning. What you don't see is the amount of work behind it.

In an atelier, a single garment can involve fittings, draping, hand embroidery and hours spent adjusting details that most people will never notice. A sleeve has to fall exactly right. A seam needs to disappear. Even a tiny change in fabric can alter the whole silhouette.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/86840ce59dd628fc3e53a537f383a5d1.jpg]]

Chanel is a particularly interesting house to look at because its codes are so recognisable. Gabrielle Chanel's little black dresses and tailored suits changed the way women dressed. Later, Karl Lagerfeld took the tweed, pearls and familiar shapes and pushed them in new directions, especially in the theatrical runway shows of the 1990s.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/018-Chanel-Couture-Jewellery-vogue-200121-credit-Getty-Images.webp]]

But couture isn't only about famous houses or extravagant designs. It's about keeping specialised skills alive. The people working behind the scenes are as important to the finished piece as the designer who imagined it.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/chanel-behind-the-scenes.jpg]]

That's why I find the backstage photographs almost as compelling as the runway images. They show a garment in progress, still being pinned, adjusted and handled with care.

Fashion moves quickly. Couture gives us a reason to look closely, and to appreciate how much can go into something that appears effortless for a few seconds on a runway.

issues.title: THE ARCHIVE
issues.subtitle: Back to the 1990s, and the clothes, photographs and effortless attitude that made Kate Moss a fashion reference.

articles.title: The Kate Moss Effect
articles.excerpt: Slip dresses, vintage coats and the art of making an outfit look entirely your own.
articles.body:
The Kate Moss Effect

Kate Moss has been a fashion reference for so long that it's easy to forget how different she looked when she first appeared in the early 1990s.

At a time when supermodels were associated with glossy hair, dramatic makeup and larger-than-life glamour, Moss brought something more undone. Her style was less about looking perfectly dressed and more about wearing things in a way that felt natural to her.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/1429652993.webp]]

The pieces themselves were often simple: slip dresses, jeans, camisoles, vintage coats and little black dresses. But the combinations made them memorable. A delicate dress with worn-in shoes. A luxurious coat over something completely ordinary. Hair that looked better slightly messy.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/34740324da86f8929382375e43915800.jpg]]

It's the contrast that keeps her wardrobe interesting. She could look glamorous without seeming overly formal, or casual without looking careless. The clothes never appeared to be wearing her.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/GettyImages-535831052.webp]]

You can see that influence in today's renewed interest in 1990s fashion, especially in vintage slips, simple tailoring and minimal makeup. Not every look has aged in the same way, and the decade had its own complicated beauty standards. Still, the styling remains worth studying.

What I take from the Kate Moss archive isn't a shopping list. It's the reminder that the way you put clothes together can be more memorable than the clothes themselves.

issues.title: THE ART OF EFFORTLESS STYLE
issues.subtitle: Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, Isabel Marant, a remarkable Hermès building and the question of what makes style personal.

articles.title: The Carolyn Bessette Effect
articles.excerpt: The coats, shirts and small styling decisions that keep her 1990s wardrobe relevant.
articles.body:
The Carolyn Bessette Effect

Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy's wardrobe is everywhere again, and I understand why. Almost every photograph offers a different lesson in how to wear very simple clothes exceptionally well.

Before her marriage to John F. Kennedy Jr., she worked at Calvin Klein, where clean lines and thoughtful proportions were part of the visual language. You can see that influence in her personal wardrobe: black coats, crisp shirts, slip dresses, straight skirts and hardly any unnecessary detail.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/may-carolyn-1.jpg]]

But copying the individual pieces doesn't quite capture what made her style interesting. It was the way she wore them. A coat left open, a headband with an otherwise plain outfit, sunglasses that made even a quick walk through New York look editorial.

The renewed attention around *Love Story* in 2026 has sent a new audience back to her archive. Some images have been shared so often they feel familiar even to people who weren't alive when they were taken.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/may-carolyn-2.jpg]]

There's a temptation to turn her style into a formula: buy a black coat, wear a white shirt, add narrow sunglasses. But what made her memorable was that she seemed to know what she liked. She repeated pieces, kept things simple and didn't appear to dress for every new trend.

That's a much more useful idea to borrow than any single outfit.

articles.title: The Isabel Marant Effect
articles.excerpt: Embroidery, ankle boots and the slightly undone side of Parisian dressing.
articles.body:
The Isabel Marant Effect

Isabel Marant has always made clothes that look as though they belong to someone with somewhere to be. They're relaxed, a little bohemian and often more interesting because they aren't perfectly polished.

She began with the label Twen in 1989 and established her namesake brand in 1995. By the 2000s, the combination of embroidered jackets, short dresses, ankle boots and easy layering had become instantly recognisable.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/may-marant-2.jpg]]

What makes the clothes work is the balance. A romantic blouse might be worn with denim. An embroidered jacket sits over a plain T-shirt. Something delicate is usually paired with something tougher, so the outfit never feels too precious.

The archives from the late 2000s and early 2010s are particularly fun to revisit. There's texture everywhere, from washed fabrics to intricate stitching, but the silhouettes still look wearable.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/may-marant-3.jpg]]

And then there was the Bekett wedge sneaker. It's hard to think of another shoe that captures the early 2010s quite so completely. You might not want to bring it back, but you can't deny it had a moment.

With the house entering a new chapter under Kim Bekker, the old collections are worth another look. They're a reminder that personal style doesn't always come from being minimal. Sometimes it comes from knowing how to mix things that shouldn't quite go together.

articles.title: When Fashion Becomes Architecture
articles.excerpt: A closer look at the glass-block Maison Hermès building in Tokyo.
articles.body:
When Fashion Becomes Architecture

Maison Hermès in Tokyo is one of those buildings that makes you stop and look up, even if you didn't come to shop.

Opened in Ginza in 2001, it was designed by Renzo Piano with Rena Dumas. Instead of a conventional storefront, the building is wrapped in translucent glass blocks. In daylight, the surface catches the changing light of the street. At night, it glows from within.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/may-hermes-2.jpg]]

It's a striking idea, but not a loud one. The facade is made of repeating elements, each one simple on its own. Together, they create something distinctive, a little like the way a beautifully made accessory depends on details you might not notice immediately.

That's the connection I find interesting between fashion and architecture. Both involve proportion, material and the decision of what to leave out. The building doesn't need a giant logo to communicate the world of Hermès.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/may-hermes-3.jpg]]

It has also been home to cultural spaces, including the Le Forum exhibition gallery and Le Studio cinema, which makes it more than a place to display products.

Luxury architecture can sometimes feel designed mainly to be photographed. Maison Hermès offers something quieter: a building that changes with the light, rewards a closer look and still feels modern more than two decades after it opened.

articles.title: Style Is Personal, Trends Are Temporary
articles.excerpt: Trends are fun to try. Building a wardrobe that feels like yours is the interesting part.
articles.body:
Style Is Personal, Trends Are Temporary

One week everyone wants a perfectly minimal wardrobe. The next, it's colour, lace, oversized jewellery or a shoe you were certain you'd never wear. Fashion is allowed to change its mind. You don't have to change yours every time.

I love looking at trends, especially old ones coming back in unexpected ways. But there's a difference between finding something inspiring and feeling as though you need to buy it before it disappears from your feed.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/may-style-2.jpg]]

The wardrobes I keep returning to are rarely built around a single trend. Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy's clean tailoring and Isabel Marant's relaxed, embroidered looks are completely different, yet both feel personal. You can tell there's a point of view behind them.

Developing your own style is mostly trial and error. You wear something, realise you love it, then reach for it again. You buy something else and discover it looked better on the moodboard. Slowly, you start to notice which colours, shapes and details actually suit your life.

[[image:https://maisonverve.github.io/maison-verve/may-style-3.jpg]]

A favourite jacket worn for years can be more useful than five new pieces bought for a particular aesthetic. And repeating outfits is not a failure of creativity. Often, it's a sign that you've found something that works.

Trends are fun to borrow from. The trick is remembering you can always give them back.

issues.title: THE SPRING AWAKENING
issues.subtitle: Spring days, soft clothes, fresh fragrances and rooms with their windows open to the garden.

articles.title: The Art of Living Slowly
articles.excerpt: Open windows, garden mornings and finding a little more time for ordinary things.
articles.body:
The Art of Living Slowly

Spring makes me want to open every window in the house. The light changes, the mornings feel less rushed and suddenly even breakfast seems nicer when there's fresh air coming in.

I've been thinking about the appeal of simple routines: flowers on the table, a walk before the day gets busy, or taking a little longer over coffee instead of checking a phone immediately. None of these things is particularly impressive, which is probably the point.

[[image:https://maisonverve.club/april-slow-2.jpg]]

Gwyneth Paltrow's interest in gardening and home life is one version of this mood. There's something appealing about growing your own herbs, spending time outside and treating the home as a place to enjoy rather than just keep tidy. You don't need a huge garden to borrow the idea. A pot of basil on the windowsill counts.

Spring also makes it easier to appreciate the little changes around you. A room looks different with the curtains open. A familiar walk suddenly has flowers along the way. Even the same old white shirt feels new after months of winter clothes.

[[image:https://maisonverve.club/april-slow-1.jpg]]

Slowing down doesn't have to mean abandoning plans or becoming a different person. Sometimes it just means paying attention to what you're already doing.

And on a sunny afternoon, with nowhere you urgently need to be, that can feel like enough.

articles.title: The Romance of Spring Dressing
articles.excerpt: White cotton, soft knits, a little lace and the joy of dressing for warmer days.
articles.body:
The Romance of Spring Dressing

The first warm days of spring always make getting dressed feel easier. Heavy layers go back into the wardrobe, white cotton comes out again and suddenly the simplest outfits are the ones I want to wear.

A little lace, a silk skirt, a soft knit or a cotton dress can make an outfit feel romantic without looking overly dressed up. The nicest combinations tend to have a bit of contrast: a delicate skirt with a simple top, or a pretty blouse with trousers you've owned for years.

[[image:https://maisonverve.club/april-fashion-2.jpg]]

Texture does a lot of the work. Broderie anglaise, linen and lightweight knits make even neutral colours interesting. And when the fabric already has detail, there's no need for complicated accessories.

Ballet flats, small gold earrings and a woven bag are easy additions, but spring dressing shouldn't feel like a checklist. A favourite pair of sandals or an old cardigan can be just as good.

[[image:https://maisonverve.club/april-fashion-3.jpg]]

I also love the softer palette that comes back at this time of year: ivory, pale pink, butter yellow and faded blue. Not because bright colours are wrong for spring, but because these shades are so easy to wear together.

The best spring wardrobe isn't necessarily a new one. It's often just a different way of wearing the things you already love.

articles.title: What Does Spring Smell Like?
articles.excerpt: Fig leaves, clean musk, soft florals and the perfumes that feel right for spring.
articles.body:
What Does Spring Smell Like?

If spring had a scent, I don't think it would be a huge bouquet of flowers. It would be the smell of a garden after rain, freshly washed sheets, a window left open and something green growing nearby.

That's the mood I look for in a spring perfume: fresh, a little soft and interesting enough that you want to smell your wrist again later.

[[image:https://maisonverve.club/april-perfume-2.jpg]]

Diptyque's Philosykos is a lovely example of a green fragrance. It brings to mind the whole fig tree, not just the fruit. Le Labo's Thé Matcha 26 is quieter and warmer, with a close-to-the-skin quality that makes it easy to wear. Maison Francis Kurkdjian's Aqua Universalis goes in a cleaner, brighter direction, while Jo Malone's Wild Bluebell offers something more floral and airy.

They're quite different fragrances, which is why I don't think spring needs one particular perfume profile. Some people want citrus and clean musk. Others love delicate flowers or soft woods.

[[image:https://maisonverve.club/april-perfume-3.jpg]]

It's also worth remembering that the best smells of the season don't come in bottles. Fresh herbs in the kitchen, cut flowers by the bed or that first moment outside after a shower can be just as memorable.

Maybe that's what I like about spring fragrances. They're less about making an entrance and more about finding a scent that feels good to live in.

articles.title: A Room with a Garden View
articles.excerpt: French doors, natural fabrics and interiors that let the garden take centre stage.
articles.body:
A Room with a Garden View

A room with a view of the garden is hard to beat. Not necessarily a grand conservatory or a perfectly landscaped estate. Even a small window with a glimpse of trees can change how a space feels.

I love interiors that make the outside feel close. French doors left open on a warm afternoon, curtains moving slightly in the breeze, sunlight falling across wooden floors. They're simple details, but they make a room feel lived in.

[[image:https://maisonverve.club/april-room-2.jpg]]

The best garden-facing spaces usually don't compete with the view. Pale walls, linen upholstery, natural wood and a few well-chosen pieces let the greenery do most of the decorating. You don't need a floral print on every surface when there are actual flowers outside.

Older houses often get this balance right. Deep window seats, tall doors and slightly imperfect materials give the room character without making it feel overly styled.

[[image:https://maisonverve.club/april-room-3.jpg]]

And there's something lovely about a space that changes throughout the day. Morning light might reach the breakfast table, while the garden looks completely different in the late afternoon.

A beautiful room isn't only about the furniture inside it. Sometimes its best feature is what you can see when you look out.
